title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Pointer
summary: Defines a string syntax for identifying a specific value inside a JSON document, using slash-separated reference tokens that walk down through objects and arrays.

plainLanguage.summary: An address that tells you which drawer, which folder and which page in a huge filing cabinet holds the thing you want.

questions: how to reference a value in a json document
what does ~1 mean in json pointer
how to use json pointer in a url fragment
subtitle: A short string syntax for pointing at one specific value inside a JSON document.

tldr.problem: There was no standard way to name one particular value inside a JSON document, either in a JSON string or in a URI fragment identifier.
tldr.mechanism: A JSON Pointer is a string of zero or more reference tokens, each prefixed by '/'. Each token steps from the current value to an object member or an array element, starting at the document root.
tldr.outcome: The same pointer can be written as a JSON string or, with percent-encoding, as a URI fragment. What happens when a pointer fails to resolve is left to the application that uses it.

today: RFC 6901 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Applications that use it must still define how to handle pointers that do not resolve.

sections.title: What JSON Pointer Is
sections.content:
RFC 6901 defines JSON Pointer, a string syntax for identifying a specific value within a JSON document. It is meant to be easy to write inside JSON string values and also inside URI fragment identifiers.

The RFC uses the RFC 2119 key words (MUST, SHOULD and so on) and writes its syntax rules in ABNF.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way to write down the address of one item inside a big pile of JSON data, so a program can find it again.

sections.title: Pointer Syntax
sections.content:
A JSON Pointer is a Unicode string made of zero or more reference tokens, each prefixed by a / character. The empty string is therefore a valid pointer. Pointers are specified in characters, not bytes.

Two characters have special meaning: ~ and /. When they appear inside a reference token, ~ is written as ~0 and / is written as ~1.

A pointer that does not match this syntax is an error condition.
sections.plainLanguage: Each step in the address starts with a slash, like folders on a computer. If a folder name itself has a slash or a squiggle in it, you write it with a special code so it does not get confused.

sections.title: Evaluating a Pointer
sections.content:
Evaluation starts at the root value of the document and handles each reference token in turn. For each token, any escape sequences are decoded first: ~1 becomes /, and only then ~0 becomes ~. The order matters. Doing it the other way would turn ~01 into ~1 and then wrongly into /; the correct result is ~1.

If the current value is a JSON object, the token names a member. The member name must match the token exactly, character for character, and no Unicode normalization is performed. If the member name is not unique in the object, the referenced member is undefined and evaluation fails.

If the current value is an array, the token MUST be either digits giving a zero-based index with no leading zeros, or the single hyphen character. The hyphen refers to the nonexistent member after the last element, so using it always produces an error unless the application says how to treat it.
sections.plainLanguage: You start at the front door and follow the address one step at a time. For a list, you say which number in the list, counting from zero. You cannot use an item that is not there.

sections.title: Pointers Inside JSON Strings
sections.content:
A pointer can be carried in a JSON string value. The usual JSON escaping applies: quotation mark, reverse solidus and control characters MUST be escaped. Backslash escape sequences must be unescaped before the string is processed as a JSON Pointer.

The RFC gives an example document with keys such as foo, the empty string, a/b, m~n and a single space. The pointer "" is the whole document, /foo/0 is "bar", / is the empty-named member whose value is 0, /a~1b is 1 and /m~0n is 8.
sections.plainLanguage: When the address is written inside a JSON message, you first undo the message's own quoting tricks, and only then read the address.

sections.title: Pointers in URI Fragments
sections.content:
A pointer can also be a URI fragment identifier. It is encoded as UTF-8 octets, and any characters not allowed in a fragment by RFC 3986 are percent-encoded. For the same example document, #/c%25d refers to the value of c%d, and #/%20 refers to the member whose name is a single space.

A media type must say explicitly that JSON Pointer is its fragment syntax, usually in its registration. Being JSON does not imply it. In particular, the fragment identifier syntax for application/json is not JSON Pointer.
sections.plainLanguage: On a web address, a few characters cannot be typed as they are, so they get swapped for a percent code. It is the same address in a different outfit.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
When an error occurs, evaluation of the pointer fails to complete. Errors include, but are not limited to, invalid pointer syntax and a pointer that references a nonexistent value.

The RFC does not define how errors are handled. An application of JSON Pointer SHOULD specify the impact and handling of each type of error. Some applications might stop processing, while others might recover by inserting default values.
sections.plainLanguage: If the address points to nothing, the finder stops. What to do next is up to whoever is using the address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A pointer is not guaranteed to reference an actual JSON value, so applications should define how an unresolved pointer is handled.

Pointers can contain the NUL character (U+0000). Care is needed in programming languages that use NUL to mark the end of a string, so that the character is not misinterpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not assume the address always leads somewhere, and be careful with one invisible character that some programs treat as the end of the writing.

data.title: JSON Pointer grammar
data.code:
json-pointer    = *( "/" reference-token )
reference-token = *( unescaped / escaped )
unescaped       = %x00-2E / %x30-7D / %x7F-10FFFF
  ; %x2F ('/') and %x7E ('~') are excluded from 'unescaped'
escaped         = "~" ( "0" / "1" )
  ; representing '~' and '/', respectively
